questions.text: What is the "controller" that you mention restarting? What does it do, and is it what moves the flag when a person advances or when a rollback finishes?
questions.about: Where the rollout state lives: Rollback progress

questions.text: When a person advances from `shadow` to `both`, what exactly happens to in-flight work? Who stops charging, and what is the new engine's first charge based on?
questions.about: shadow --> both : person advances. Gate A met

questions.text: What is the "shadow store" and the "usage log"? Where does each live, and who writes to and reads from them?
In `both`, how does the old engine compute into the shadow store while the new engine charges? Where does the old engine get its inputs, and does it matter that it is not charging?
questions.about: both row in What each mode does

questions.text: In `new_only` the old engine is stopped. What does "skipped events" mean, and how does the old engine know which events it skipped during catch up?
questions.about: Rollback 2: old engine reprocesses skipped events

questions.text: In the rollback from `both`, the old engine was computing but not charging. Why is there no catch up step there, and where does the shadow store come from in that case?
questions.about: which_mode choice: rolling back from both

questions.text: In reconcile, how does a period get marked "due-and-uncharged" versus "charged" when the in-flight outcome is unknown? What do you do to resolve it, and what if the provider cannot say?
Who measures the charge failure rate, from what data, and what counts as a failure? Does the 2% need a minimum number of charges?
questions.about: Charge failure rate above 2% over any 10-minute window

answers.text: The controller is the service that will be built after this model. It moves the flag when a person advances and when a rollback finishes, runs the rollback steps, evaluates the automatic trigger and keeps the rollback record. Decided because the flag and the rollback record need exactly one owner. Now defined in the terms.

No freeze on a forward move. The controller sets the flag, charges the previous charger already started finish, and the new charger charges only periods with no charge under the customer plus billing period idempotency key. Workers check the key against the ledger and provider before charging. Reason: the key already prevents double charges, and a freeze would delay charges for no gain. Listed as an assumption to confirm.

The usage log is the existing event log (kept 35 days) read by both engines. The shadow store is the separate store written only by the non-charging engine and read only by the nightly comparison. The brief does not say where the shadow store physically lives or what technology it is. Added to open questions, and both defined in the terms.

The brief says the old engine keeps computing every invoice into the shadow store in both. It reads the same usage log as the new engine. Not charging does not change how it computes; the invoices are only used for the nightly comparison. Stated in the both row of the table.

Skipped events are the usage events that arrived after the old engine stopped on entering new_only. The old engine knows where to resume from a checkpoint, its last processed position in the usage log, which stays fixed while it is stopped. Decided because it is the simplest way to know what was skipped; the brief gives no mechanism. Added the checkpoint to the terms, the table and the state section.
In both the old engine kept computing every invoice into the shadow store, so it has skipped nothing and the shadow store is already current. No catch up is needed. Added to rollback step 2.

A period is charged if the provider shows a charge for its key (the ledger entry is added if missing). It is due-and-uncharged if neither shows a charge. An in-flight charge with unknown outcome is resolved by asking the provider by key. If the provider cannot say, the period stays unresolved, is not charged, and on-call is paged. Reason: a late charge is recoverable, a double charge is not. How long to wait is an open question.

The brief does not say. I assume the controller computes it from the new engine's charge attempt results, but the definition of a failure (provider errors only, or customer declines too) and whether a minimum number of charges is needed to avoid noise at low volume are not decided. Added to open questions.

questions.text: What makes a period become due, and what starts a charge? Is it a schedule at period end, or does an engine charge as usage events arrive?
questions.about: Rollback 4: hand charging to old engine

questions.text: Where does the old engine get the invoice amount it charges in hand over? Is it the one it computed into the shadow store, and does it get used even though the shadow store is never treated as truth?
questions.about: Rollback 4: hand charging to old engine

questions.text: Reconcile marks periods once. What happens to a period that falls due after reconcile has finished but before the flag is set to old_only?
How does a mismatch get resolved, who resolves it, and where is that recorded so the gate counter knows?
questions.about: Gate B: 14 days in both with no unresolved mismatches

questions.text: How does the new engine's workers learn to freeze when the flag still says both or new_only? What signal do they read, and who sets it?
When the flag changes, how do the workers of the old charger know to stop starting new charges? Do they just read the flag, and what if some still have the old value?
questions.about: Advancing: no freeze on a forward move

questions.text: How does on-call start a manual rollback? Do they call the controller, and does the controller check that the person is allowed to?

answers.text: The brief does not say what makes a period due or whether charging runs on a schedule at period end or as events arrive. The model only relies on each period being charged once under its key. Added to open questions.

The old engine charges its own computed invoice for the period (from catch up, or from computing continuously in both). The shadow store is only where that invoice is kept. 'Never treated as truth' means whether a period is already charged is decided from the ledger and provider only. Reason: the old engine is the only source of its own amounts, and the ledger and provider guard against double charges. Stated in step 4.

A period that falls due after reconcile but before the flag changes is held by the freeze. Hand over charges it too, after checking its key against the ledger and provider. Reason: it is due and uncharged, and the key check stops a double charge. This was a real gap; step 4 now says it.
The brief says 'no unresolved mismatches' but not how a mismatch is resolved, by whom, or where that is recorded. I will not invent a mechanism. Added to open questions.

The controller sets a frozen marker in the rollback record, and the new engine's workers read that record, as well as the flag, before starting each charge. Reason: the flag has only four values and must not change until hand over, so the freeze needs its own signal, and the rollback record already exists. Step 1 and the state section now say this.

Yes, workers read the flag before starting each charge. A worker that still has the old value is not stopped by the flag but by the key check against the ledger and provider, which is why that check exists. Reason: no freeze on forward moves, so the key is the safety net. Stated under Advancing.

On-call sends the request to the controller, which refuses anyone not allowed to make it. Reason: the controller already owns the flag and the rollback record, so it should be the single entry point. How people are identified is not designed here and is listed as an assumption.

teachbacks.text:
1. Starting point: billing_mode is old_only. Billing workers run the old engine. It reads usage events from the usage log (35-day retention), advances its checkpoint, computes invoices, writes the billing ledger, and charges customers through the payment provider. The new engine is off.

2. Advance to shadow. A person sends a request to the rollout controller. The controller refuses anyone not allowed. If the request is allowed, the controller sets billing_mode=shadow in the config service. Nothing freezes on a forward move. Workers read the flag before each charge and may see the change at different moments. The old engine still computes, charges and writes the ledger. The new engine now reads the same usage events and writes its invoices only to the shadow store, never to the ledger and never charging. New-engine errors here are only recorded and cause no rollback.

3. Nightly comparison. Each night a job compares the two engines' invoices per customer. A mismatch is a totals difference of more than one cent. Results feed the gate counters: consecutive days, invoices compared, mismatch rate and open mismatches. If the job fails or is skipped, that day does not count and the consecutive-day count breaks.

4. Advance to both (Gate A). Gate A needs 7 consecutive days under 0.1% mismatch and at least 5,000 invoices compared. A person asks the controller, which sets the flag to both. Charges the old engine already started finish. For each new charge, a worker reads the flag, and also checks the idempotency key (customer plus billing period) against the ledger and the provider. A worker still holding the old flag value is stopped by that key check. The new engine now computes, charges and writes the ledger. The old engine keeps computing every invoice into the shadow store so it stays current. The controller records the mode-change timestamp, and the days in both are counted from it.

5. Normal charging in both. The new engine sends the charge to the payment provider with the key. The provider applies a repeated key once. The ledger is the system of record. Nightly comparison now compares old against new. If the charge failure rate exceeds 2% over any 10-minute window, the controller starts an automatic rollback at rollback step 1 (see step 9).

6. Advance to new_only (Gate B). Gate B needs 14 days in both with no unresolved mismatches, plus Finance sign-off. A person asks the controller, which sets the flag to new_only. The old engine stops and its checkpoint stays where it was. The new engine keeps charging and writing the ledger. Days in new_only are counted from the mode-change timestamp.

7. Commit. At day 35 in new_only the state becomes committed. The usage log has expired the oldest skipped events, so the old engine can no longer catch up and rollback is closed. A failure after that pages on-call to fix forward. Decommissioning the old engine is a separate action a person takes later.

8. Manual rollback from shadow. On-call asks the controller. Since the new engine never charged, there are no rollback steps. The flag goes to old_only. Gates reset, so the 7-day count starts at zero.

9. Rollback from both or new_only. It starts when on-call asks manually, or when the controller's automatic trigger fires. A trigger arriving mid-rollback is ignored. The controller keeps a durable rollback record holding the current step, origin, trigger and frozen state. A restarted controller resumes from it.
   - Step 1, freeze. The controller marks the record frozen. The new engine's workers read the record as well as the flag before each charge and start none. In-flight charges finish. Due charges are held, not dropped. The flag does not change here.
   - Step 2, catch up (new_only only). The old engine reprocesses every usage event after its checkpoint into the shadow store. This only works inside the 35-day window. From both this step is skipped.
   - Step 3, reconcile. For each customer and period, the ledger is compared with the provider. If the provider shows a charge for the key, the period is charged, and the ledger entry is added if missing. If neither shows a charge, the period is due-and-uncharged. For an in-flight charge of unknown outcome, ask the provider by key. If the provider cannot say, the period stays unresolved, is not charged, and on-call is paged.
   - Step 4, hand over. The old engine charges the due-and-uncharged periods, plus any held after reconcile finished. It uses the same key, checks the ledger and provider first, and uses its own computed invoice amount. Then the flag is set to old_only and the freeze is cleared. Gates reset.

10. After rollback. The only way forward is old_only to shadow, triggered by a person, with the gate counters starting from zero.

11. Failures during rollback. If a step fails or stalls, it is retried (steps are safe to repeat). The flag does not move, charging stays frozen and on-call is paged. Held charges are late, not lost, and nobody is charged twice. If the config service is unreachable, workers keep their last known mode and must never fall back to a default.
gaps: What starts a charge and what makes a billing period due (schedule at period end, or as events arrive) is not stated. I cannot say what triggers the worker's charge in steps 2 to 5.
How a mismatch becomes resolved for Gate B, who resolves it, and where that is recorded.
What counts as a charge failure for the 2% auto-rollback trigger, who measures it, and whether a minimum number of charges is needed. I cannot say exactly when the automatic rollback fires.
What happens if a catch-up rollback cannot finish before events expire at day 35.
What happens when the provider cannot report an in-flight charge's outcome for a long time. The rollback waits and pages on-call, but there is no resolution path.
How the controller identifies and authorises people and on-call. It is not designed, so I cannot explain how the refusal works.
How the nightly comparison, Finance sign-off and the 'person advances' request reach the controller. The channel and interface are unspecified.
